claims.text: The simulated alloy is equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
Equiatomic FeNiCrMn has a single-phase FCC initial structure.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure contains inherent chemical short-range order.
The initial structure has no pre-existing vacancy clusters or twin boundaries.
FeNiCrMn yield strength is nearly insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
The strain-rate insensitivity arises because an SRO-controlled energy barrier governs dislocation nucleation rather than thermal activation or vacancy-cluster availability.
SRO clusters are the primary nucleation barrier for Shockley partial dislocations in FeNiCrMn.
Dislocation nucleation occurs at interfaces of SRO clusters.
Local lattice distortion at SRO-cluster interfaces creates the critical stress concentration for nucleation.
The energy barrier for breaking SRO bonds dominates over thermal activation throughout the simulated strain-rate window.
Loading along <11-1> produces a higher maximum yield stress than loading along <110>.
The higher stress for <11-1> results from alignment of the slip-plane normal with the loading axis, which maximizes resolved shear stress.
The orientation dependence follows the Schmid factor for the FCC {111}<110> slip system.
Dislocation density increases with strain rate even though yield strength remains nearly constant.
Dislocation nucleation sites correlate spatially with SRO regions rather than vacancy clusters.
Standard FCC deformation is typically strain-rate sensitive because dislocation sources are thermally activated.
Frank-Read sources and vacancy-assisted nucleation are representative thermally activated sources in standard FCC deformation.
Cryogenic conditions can promote twinning in compositionally similar alloys.
At strain rates above 10^10 s^-1, thermal activation may become negligible.
SRO exists in CrCoNi and correlates with its mechanical properties, including increased hardness or strength relative to a random alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says alignment of a slip-plane normal with the loading axis maximizes resolved shear stress, while the mechanism invokes the Schmid factor. Exact normal-axis alignment gives a zero plane-direction cosine product for slip within that plane, rather than a maximum Schmid factor, so the stated geometric explanation does not coherently support the orientation ranking.
